items.stem: Analyse the reasons why Watergate led to Nixon's resignation.
items.answer: Investigations by the press, the courts and the Senate. The existence of the White House tapes. The Supreme Court's ruling in United States v. Nixon. The loss of support among Republicans in Congress. Nixon's own decision to cover up the break-in. Judgement: the cover-up, exposed by the tapes, destroyed Nixon's support and made impeachment certain.

items.stem: Mohammed is planning an answer to the question: “‘Watergate permanently weakened the American presidency.’ How far do you agree?” Write a one-sentence line of argument for the answer and outline two points Mohammed could use to support the view and two to challenge it.
items.answer: Line of argument: Watergate weakened the presidency in the 1970s, but the effect was not permanent, as Reagan showed. Support: Congress passed the War Powers Act and the Budget and Impoundment Control Act. Public trust in government fell sharply. Challenge: Reagan restored presidential authority in the 1980s. Presidents continued to use military force without declarations.
items.markingKey: 2 marks for a line of argument that answers the question directly and is sustainable; 1 mark for each relevant supporting point and 1 for each challenging point [6]

items.stem: On 17 June 1972 five men were arrested breaking into the Democratic National Committee offices in the Watergate building. How far was Nixon a successful president apart from Watergate?
items.answer: For: Détente with the USSR and the opening to China. The EPA and environmental laws. The end of US ground involvement in Vietnam. Against: The war was extended to Cambodia and Laos. Inflation and economic problems. His methods and abuse of power. Judgement: Nixon had real achievements, especially in foreign policy, but his abuses of power define his presidency.

Level 4 (13-16): analysis of both sides with a judgement, though not fully sustained or supported. Level 3 (9-12): some analysis, but one-sided or uneven, or with descriptive passages. Level 2 (5-8): mainly descriptive or narrative, with limited links to the question. Level 1 (1-4): general, unsupported or irrelevant points. The end of US ground involvement in Vietnam. Disagree / other factors: The war was extended to Cambodia and Laos. Inflation and economic problems. His methods and abuse of power. Possible judgement: Nixon had real achievements, especially in foreign policy, but his abuses of power define his presidency. [20]

items.stem: Put these events in chronological order, starting with the earliest. A: The Iran-Contra affair became public. B: The Iran hostage crisis began. C: Reagan defeated Carter. D: Carter became president.
items.answer: D, B, C, A (D January 1977; B November 1979; C November 1980; A November 1986)
items.markingKey: Correct order D, B, C, A (D January 1977; B November 1979; C November 1980; A November 1986): 2 marks if all correct, 1 mark if one adjacent pair is reversed. [2]

items.stem: Amara is planning an answer to the question: “‘Reagan restored the power and prestige of the presidency.’ How far do you agree?” Write a one-sentence line of argument for the answer and outline two points Amara could use to support the view and two to challenge it.
items.answer: Line of argument: Reagan restored confidence in the presidency after the 1970s, though Iran-Contra showed the risks of its power. Support: He won landslides in 1980 and 1984. He passed major tax cuts and set the political agenda. Challenge: Iran-Contra showed abuse of power. Congress remained Democratic in the House and limited him.
items.markingKey: 2 marks for a line of argument that answers the question directly and is sustainable; 1 mark for each relevant supporting point and 1 for each challenging point [6]

items.stem: Mateo is planning an answer to the question: “How far did conservatism dominate American politics, 1977-93?” Write a one-sentence line of argument for the answer and outline two points Mateo could use to support the view and two to challenge it.
items.answer: Line of argument: conservatism dominated the presidency and the political agenda, but not the whole system. Support: Reagan won two landslides and Bush won in 1988. Tax cuts and deregulation reshaped policy. Challenge: Democrats controlled the House throughout. Social Security and Medicare remained.

items.stem: Mei is planning an answer to the question: “How far did Eisenhower change the role of the presidency?” Write a one-sentence line of argument for the answer and outline two points Mei could use to support the view and two to challenge it.
items.answer: Line of argument: Eisenhower consolidated rather than changed the presidency, using its powers cautiously. Support: He used a "hidden-hand" style of leadership. He sent troops to Little Rock. Challenge: He accepted the New Deal settlement. He was reluctant to act on civil rights.

items.stem: Study Sources C and D. Source C: Joseph McCarthy, speech at Wheeling, West Virginia, February 1950 (summary). McCarthy claimed that he had a list of people in the State Department known to be members of the Communist Party; the number he gave changed in later accounts. Source D: a poll report, 1950 (illustrative). “Since the news from China and the Soviet bomb, more than half of those asked believe that communists in government are a serious danger to the country.” Compare and contrast Sources C and D as evidence about McCarthyism.
items.answer: Source C: It shows McCarthy making dramatic but unproven accusations. Source D: It suggests international events increased fear of communists at home. They should be compared on what each says about McCarthyism; similarities and differences should be supported with details. Provenance: C is Joseph McCarthy, speech at Wheeling, West Virginia, February 1950 (summary) (he could not substantiate his claims and changed the figures); D is a poll report, 1950 (illustrative) (the wording of questions shapes the answers). Differences in authorship, date and purpose explain the contrast.
items.markingKey: Level 4 (12-15): compares and contrasts the sources, explaining similarities AND differences, and evaluates them using provenance and context to explain why they differ. Level 3 (8-11): explains similarities AND differences in content, supported by details from both sources. Level 2 (4-7): explains a similarity OR a difference. Level 1 (1-3): describes or paraphrases the content of the sources without valid comparison. [15]

items.stem: What is meant by “Gulf of Tonkin Resolution”?
options: The 1973 law limiting the president's power to commit troops without Congress.
The 1964 resolution giving Johnson power to use force in Vietnam.
The use of reckless accusations of communist sympathy, especially by Senator McCarthy in 1950-54.
Truman's programme of social reforms, many of which Congress rejected.
items.answer: The 1964 resolution giving Johnson power to use force in Vietnam.
items.markingKey: Gulf of Tonkin Resolution: the 1964 resolution giving Johnson power to use force in Vietnam. [1]

items.stem: Which of these statements is accurate?
options: Nixon was impeached and removed from office by the Senate.
McCarthy exposed large numbers of communist spies in the State Department.
The Gulf of Tonkin Resolution increased presidential power over the use of force.
items.answer: The Gulf of Tonkin Resolution increased presidential power over the use of force.
items.markingKey: It allowed Johnson to escalate the war without a declaration. The other statements are inaccurate. [1]

items.stem: Historians have offered several reasons why Johnson was able to pass so much legislation in 1964-65. A: Sympathy after Kennedy's assassination. B: Economic growth made spending affordable. C: Pressure from the civil rights movement. Explain how these reasons were linked and decide which mattered most.
items.answer: Any reasoned choice. A: Sympathy after Kennedy's assassination. B: Economic growth made spending affordable. C: Pressure from the civil rights movement. Possible judgement: Johnson's legislative skill combined with exceptional political circumstances in 1964-65.
items.markingKey: 1 mark for a choice; up to 3 marks for explaining it with precise detail; up to 2 marks for comparing it with the other reasons [6]

items.stem: Read the sources carefully. Source A: Lyndon Johnson, speech at the University of Michigan, May 1964 (summary). Johnson described a Great Society resting on abundance and liberty for all, demanding an end to poverty and racial injustice. Source B: a memoir by a Kennedy aide, 1965 (illustrative). “The President knew what had to be done on civil rights and on poverty. The bills were written; what he lacked was time and the votes in Congress.” “Johnson was a more effective president than Kennedy in domestic policy.” How far do Sources A and B support this view?
items.answer: Source A supports: it shows Johnson's broader domestic ambition. Evaluation: it is political rhetoric. Source B challenges: it credits Kennedy with the agenda. Evaluation: written soon after the assassination by a loyal admirer. Grouping: support A; challenge B. A judgement must weigh how convincing each group is, using provenance and own knowledge, rather than counting sources.
items.markingKey: Level 5 (17-20): evaluates the sources (provenance, purpose, context, cross-reference) to show how far they support AND challenge the view, reaching a supported judgement. Level 4 (13-16): uses the sources to support AND challenge the view and evaluates some of them. Level 3 (9-12): uses the sources at face value to support AND challenge. Level 2 (5-8): uses the sources to support OR challenge. Level 1 (1-4): writes about the topic without valid use of the sources. (The examination version uses four sources and 25 marks; levels are scaled.) [20]

items.stem: Read Source B. “It is a crisis of confidence. It is a crisis that strikes at the very heart and soul and spirit of our national will.” (Jimmy Carter, televised address, July 1979 (abridged).) Assess the reliability of Source B as evidence about Carter's leadership.
items.answer: Reliable because it is the president's own analysis. Less reliable because many saw it as blaming the public, which damaged him. Cross-reference: It does not show his achievements. Judgement: reliable as evidence of this point of view, but it needs to be tested against other evidence.
